questions.question: Explain the sliding window technique in Java. Compare fixed vs variable-size windows. Solve max-sum subarray of size K and longest substring without repeating characters.
questions.title: Sliding Window Technique — Fixed vs Variable, with Java Solutions
questions.direct_answer: **Sliding window** maintains a **contiguous range** of elements and moves it through the input, **incrementally updating state** instead of recomputing from scratch. It turns O(n·k) brute force into O(n) for many contiguous-range problems. **Fixed-size window**: the window has a constant size K; slide one step at a time, adding the new element and removing the oldest (`sum = sum + arr[right] - arr[right - k]`). **Variable-size window**: the window grows/shrinks based on a condition (e.g., 'all characters unique' or 'sum ≤ target'); typically uses two pointers `left` and `right`, where `right` expands and `left` contracts when the condition is violated. Use fixed when **K is given**; use variable when you're finding **the longest/shortest window satisfying a condition**. Both are O(n) because each element enters and exits the window at most once. **When to use**: (1) problem asks for **contiguous** subarray/substring, (2) with an optimization goal (max/min/count/exists), (3) involving **sum, product, frequency, or other aggregatable** property. Common problems: max/min sum subarray of size K, longest substring without repeats, smallest subarray with sum ≥ target, longest substring with K distinct characters, permutation in string, minimum window substring. **Key insight**: avoid recomputing by **maintaining state incrementally** — add what enters, remove what exits. For frequency-based windows, use a `HashMap<Character, Integer>` or `int[]` (for ASCII). The window's state is typically a sum, product, or count map. **Don't use sliding window** for: non-contiguous problems (subset/subsequence), problems requiring random access or reordering, or problems where the 'state' can't be incrementally updated.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate can recognize sliding window problems, distinguish fixed vs variable window, implement both templates correctly, and achieve O(n) complexity
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using nested loops instead of incremental state update (O(n·k) instead of O(n)). Off-by-one in window boundaries. Forgetting to shrink the window when condition is violated
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss the amortized O(n) argument (each element enters/exits once), mention when to use HashMap vs int[] for frequency, contrast with two-pointer technique, address edge cases (empty input, K > n)

sections.title: What Sliding Window Is — The Core Idea
Fixed-Size Window — Max Sum Subarray of Size K
Variable-Size Window — Longest Substring Without Repeating
Variable Window Template — General Pattern
When to Use and Not Use
sections.content:
**Use sliding window when**:
- The input is an **array or string**.
- You need a **contiguous subarray / substring**.
- The goal is: longest, shortest, max sum, min sum, count, or 'does there exist'.
- The window state is **incrementally updatable**: sum, count, product (with caveats), frequency map.

**Don't use when**:
- Subsequence (non-contiguous) — DP or other techniques.
- Need to reorder elements — two-pointer on sorted array.
- Can't maintain state incrementally (e.g., median of window — needs two heaps, O(n log k)).
- Unbounded window that never shrinks — just a linear scan.

**Key trick for problems with duplicates / conditions**:
- 'At most K distinct' – variable window, shrink when size > K.
- 'Exactly K distinct' = 'at most K' - 'at most K-1' (subtract).
- 'All anagrams of pattern' – fixed window of size |pattern|, compare frequency.

**Common pitfalls**:
- **Off-by-one**: window size = `right - left + 1` (inclusive).
- **Forgetting to shrink**: leads to incorrect answer.
- **Integer overflow**: for product windows with negative numbers, use long.
- **Negative numbers** break monotone assumptions — standard variable window assumes positive contributions; for mixed-sign, use prefix sums + deque.
- **Empty input / K > n**: handle edge cases explicitly.

sections.title: Fixed vs Variable Window — Side by Side
sections.content:
| Property | Fixed-Size Window | Variable-Size Window |
|---|---|---|
| **Window size** | Constant K | Grows/shrinks |
| **Control** | Just `right` advances, `left = right - k + 1` | Both `left` and `right` move |
| **When to use** | K is given ("size K subarray") | Condition on window ("longest with X") |
| **State update** | Add arr[right], remove arr[right-k] | Add arr[right]; while violated, remove arr[left] |
| **Examples** | Max sum size K, anagrams, max in window | Longest unique, min subarray ≥ target, K distinct chars |
| **Time** | O(n) | O(n) amortized |
| **Template lines** | ~10 | ~15 |
| **Edge cases** | K > n, K = 0 | empty window, no valid window |

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Sliding window** turns O(n·k) brute force into O(n) for contiguous range problems.
- **Fixed-size**: window of constant size K, slide one step at a time.
- **Variable-size**: two pointers, grow `right`, shrink `left` when condition violated.
- **Time O(n)** amortized: each element enters and exits the window at most once.
- **Use cases**: contiguous subarray/substring + aggregatable property (sum, count, frequency).
- **Don't use**: non-contiguous (subsequence), unordered (use set/map), median (use two heaps).
- **Frequency tracking**: `int[]` for ASCII (faster), `HashMap` for Unicode.
- **Window size** = `right - left + 1` (inclusive).
- **Variable template**: expand, shrink-while-violated, update result.
- **'Exactly K' trick**: atMost(K) - atMost(K-1).
- **Mixed-sign arrays**: standard variable window may not apply; may need prefix sums + deque.
- **Overflow**: long for large sums/products.
- **Edge cases**: empty input, K > n, K = 0.
- **Alternative**: monotonic deque for max/min in window (O(n) amortized).
- **Related patterns**: two-pointer (sorted arrays), prefix sum (range queries).
- **Common problems**: longest substring unique, smallest subarray sum ≥ target, anagrams, minimum window substring.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Sliding window** maintains a contiguous range of elements and updates state incrementally as the window slides. Turns O(n·k) brute force into O(n).

**Two flavors**

**Fixed-size window**
- K is given
- Window size constant
- Add arr[right], remove arr[right - k]
- Track max/min/etc.

**Variable-size window**
- Two pointers left, right
- right expands, left contracts when condition violated
- Track longest/shortest/count of valid windows

**Both are O(n)**
- Each element enters and exits at most once
- Amortized linear

**When to use**
- Contiguous subarray or substring
- Optimization goal: longest, shortest, max sum, min sum, count, existence
- State is incrementally updatable (sum, count, frequency)

**When not to use**
- Non-contiguous (subsequence — use DP)
- Need reordering (use two pointers on sorted)
- State can't be updated incrementally (median — use two heaps)

**Fixed-size template (max sum subarray of size K)**

1. Compute sum of first K elements
2. For each new position: sum += arr[right] - arr[right - k]; update max
3. O(n), O(1) space

**Variable-size template (longest substring without repeating)**

1. Map<Character, Integer> lastSeen; left = 0, maxLen = 0
2. For each right: if char seen and within window, move left past it
3. Update lastSeen and maxLen

**Generic variable template**
- Expand right, update state
- While condition violated: shrink left, update state
- Update result

**Common applications**

**Sum-based**
- Max/min sum subarray of size K
- Smallest subarray with sum ≥ target
- Longest subarray with sum = K

**Character-based**
- Longest substring without repeating
- Longest substring with at most K distinct
- Longest substring with exactly K distinct (atMost(K) - atMost(K-1))
- Minimum window substring (classic hard)
- Anagrams / permutations in string

**Deque-based**
- Max in each window of size K (monotonic deque, O(n) amortized)

**Key tricks**

**Frequency map for 'at most K distinct'**
- count.merge(c, 1, Integer::sum)
- while count.size() > K: decrement/remove at left

**ASCII vs Unicode**
- int[128] or int[256] for ASCII (fast, cache-friendly)
- HashMap<Character, Integer> for Unicode

**'Exactly K' trick**
- Transform to 'at most K' minus 'at most K-1'
- Simplifies logic

**Window size formula**
- `right - left + 1` (inclusive)
- Common off-by-one mistake

**Common pitfalls**

**1. Nested loops instead of incremental update**
- Wastes the technique — O(n·k) instead of O(n)

**2. Off-by-one in window size**
- size = right - left + 1
- Not right - left

**3. Forgetting to shrink**
- Window grows unbounded — wrong result

**4. Integer overflow**
- Products with large values — use long

**5. Negative numbers**
- Standard variable window assumes monotone behavior
- With negatives, window may need shrinking even when adding helps
- Use prefix sums + deque for mixed-sign subarray sum problems

**6. Edge cases**
- Empty input
- K > n (fixed-size impossible)
- K = 0

**Recommendation:** Sliding window is one of the **most common patterns in coding interviews** — master both the **fixed** and **variable** templates because they cover 80% of contiguous-range problems. Use **fixed** when the window size is explicitly given (max sum subarray of size K, anagrams); use **variable** when searching for the **longest** or **shortest** window satisfying a condition (longest without repeating, minimum window containing all chars of T). The key insight is **incremental state maintenance**: don't recompute — add what enters, remove what exits. This gives **O(n)** amortized even when the inner logic looks like a nested loop. For **frequency tracking**, prefer **int[] over HashMap** when the alphabet is ASCII (much faster, no hashing overhead). Use the **'atMost(K) - atMost(K-1)'** trick for 'exactly K distinct' problems — it's cleaner than tracking exact-K directly. Watch for **negative numbers** in subarray-sum problems — standard variable window may fail; use **prefix sums with a monotonic deque or HashMap**. Always handle **edge cases**: empty input, K > n, K = 0. The mental model: **window = contiguous range with state; move the window, update state, record result**. Once you see a problem involving contiguous subarrays with an optimization goal, sliding window should be your first instinct.

questions.question: Explain the two-pointer technique in Java. Cover opposite-ends and same-direction variants. Solve two-sum on a sorted array and container-with-most-water.
questions.title: Two-Pointers Technique — Opposite-Ends, Same-Direction, with Java Examples
questions.direct_answer: **Two-pointer** uses two indices that traverse the array in a coordinated way, typically converging or moving in tandem, to solve problems in **O(n)** time instead of O(n²). Two main variants: **(1) Opposite ends** — `left = 0`, `right = n-1`, move them toward each other based on a condition. Used for **sorted arrays** (two-sum sorted, container with most water, palindrome check, reverse array, 3-sum). **(2) Same direction** — both pointers move forward; one (fast) leads, the other (slow) follows. Used for **in-place modification** (remove duplicates, move zeros), **linked lists** (middle, cycle detection — see Floyd's algorithm), and **streaming scans**. A **third variant**, sliding window, is sometimes classified as a two-pointer technique (both left/right move forward, like same-direction). **When to use**: (1) **sorted array** + pair/target search; (2) **palindrome**; (3) **in-place modification** where order is preserved; (4) **merge** two sorted arrays; (5) **partition** (Dutch national flag, quicksort partitioning). **Why it works**: exploits **sortedness** or **monotonicity** — moving one pointer irreversibly commits to skipping certain states, which would otherwise require nested iteration. On a **sorted array**, if `arr[left] + arr[right] > target`, decreasing `right` is safe because all pairs `(left, right_remaining)` are even smaller, so we'd never find a valid one; similarly for increasing `left` when too small. **Don't use** for: unsorted arrays without sorting first (may not find the answer), problems requiring random access patterns, or when sortedness destroys the ordering information needed. **Common complexity**: O(n) for linear passes, O(n log n) when sorting first (e.g., 3-sum).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows the two main variants, can apply the technique correctly, and explain why convergent pointers on sorted arrays achieve O(n)
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using two pointers on unsorted array without sorting first. Mixing up convergent vs same-direction. Off-by-one or infinite-loop bugs when pointers don't advance
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the monotonicity argument (why moving a pointer is safe), mention three-pointer extensions (3-sum, Dutch flag), discuss when sorting cost (O(n log n)) is justified

sections.title: The Two-Pointer Idea
sections.content:
Two-pointer is a **traversal pattern** that uses two indices to scan through data in a coordinated way — either converging from opposite ends or moving together in the same direction. It's a key tool for reducing **O(n²)** nested-loop solutions to **O(n)**.

**Two main variants**:

**1. Opposite-ends (convergent)**
```
left = 0
right = n - 1
while (left < right):
    decide whether to move left or right based on arr[left], arr[right]
```
- Use on **sorted arrays** (or palindromes, etc.).
- Classic examples: two-sum sorted, container with most water, reverse array, palindrome.

**2. Same-direction (tandem)**
```
slow = 0
for fast in 0..n-1:
    if condition: advance slow
```
- One pointer (fast) scans; the other (slow) marks a position.
- Classic examples: remove duplicates from sorted array, move zeros to end, linked list middle.

**Why it's powerful**: exploits sortedness/monotonicity to skip entire ranges of states that brute force would explore. Achieves **O(n)** with **O(1)** extra space.

sections.content:
| Property | Opposite-Ends (Convergent) | Same-Direction (Tandem) |
|---|---|---|
| **Start** | `left=0, right=n-1` | `slow=0`, `fast=0` or 1 |
| **Loop condition** | `while (left < right)` | `for fast = 0..n-1` |
| **Movement** | Pointers converge | Both move forward |
| **Used on** | Sorted arrays, palindromes | In-place mutation, streaming scans, linked lists |
| **Examples** | 2-sum sorted, container water, palindrome, reverse | Remove duplicates, move zeros, linked list middle |
| **Prerequisite** | Sortedness/monotonicity | Linear scan semantics |
| **Time** | O(n) | O(n) |
| **Space** | O(1) | O(1) |

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Two-pointer** reduces O(n²) nested-loop problems to O(n) via coordinated traversal.
- **Two variants**: opposite-ends (convergent) and same-direction (tandem).
- **Opposite-ends** requires **sortedness** or **monotonicity** to justify skipping states.
- **Same-direction** uses fast/slow pointers for in-place mutation or linked-list traversal.
- **Time O(n)**; **Space O(1)** (unless sorting first, which is O(n log n)).
- **Canonical problems**: two-sum sorted, container with most water, 3-sum, Dutch flag, remove duplicates, merge sorted.
- **For unsorted two-sum**: use HashMap (O(n) time, O(n) space) — two-pointer requires sortedness.
- **3-sum = outer loop + two-pointer on rest**: O(n²).
- **Dutch flag**: three pointers partition in O(n).
- **Linked list patterns**: slow/fast for middle, cycle detection, Kth from end.
- **Monotonicity argument**: moving the right pointer left discards states that can't improve the answer.
- **Container with most water**: always move the shorter side.
- **Common bugs**: infinite loop when neither pointer advances; off-by-one on boundaries.
- **When sorting first is worth it**: if subsequent two-pointer saves O(n²) or enables simpler logic — worth the O(n log n) upfront.
- **Compared to sliding window**: sliding window is a special case of same-direction two-pointer; both left and right advance.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Two-pointer** uses two indices traversing an array in a coordinated way to solve problems in O(n) instead of O(n²).

**Two main variants**

**1. Opposite-ends (convergent)**
- left = 0, right = n - 1
- Move toward each other based on condition
- Requires sortedness or monotonicity
- Examples: two-sum sorted, container with most water, palindrome, reverse array

**2. Same-direction (tandem)**
- Both pointers move forward
- Fast leads, slow follows
- Used for in-place modification, linked list traversal
- Examples: remove duplicates, move zeros, linked list middle

**Why opposite-ends works — the monotonicity argument**

**Two-sum sorted example**
- arr[left] + arr[right] < target: moving right left gives smaller sums (already too small); must move left right
- arr[left] + arr[right] > target: moving left right gives larger sums (already too large); must move right left
- Each move irrevocably commits to skipping pairs — safely
- Sortedness is the invariant that makes this safe

**Two-sum sorted code**
```java
while (left < right) {
    sum = arr[left] + arr[right]
    if sum == target: return answer
    else if sum < target: left++
    else right--
}
```
- O(n), O(1) space

**Container with most water**
- Area = min(h[left], h[right]) × (right - left)
- Always move the shorter side
- Why? Taller side: height capped by shorter, width smaller → only decreases; moving shorter might find taller line, potentially improving

**Same-direction pattern**

**Remove duplicates from sorted array**
- slow marks last unique position; fast scans
- When arr[fast] != arr[slow]: slow++; arr[slow] = arr[fast]
- In-place, O(n), O(1) space

**Move zeros to end**
- slow marks next non-zero position; fast scans
- Swap when arr[fast] != 0

**Linked list middle**
- slow moves 1, fast moves 2
- When fast reaches end, slow is at middle

**Three-pointer extensions**

**3-sum**
- Sort, outer loop on first index
- Two-pointer on remaining two indices
- O(n²) overall
- Skip duplicates for distinct triplets

**Dutch national flag (sort 0/1/2)**
- low, mid, high pointers
- low tracks 0-region, mid scans, high tracks 2-region
- Three-way partition in O(n)
- Lomuto partition uses similar idea for quicksort

**Merge two sorted arrays**
- Two pointers i, j on the inputs
- Write smaller to output, advance that pointer
- O(n + m)

**When to use**

**Sorted array + pair or triplet search** → opposite-ends

**Palindrome check** → opposite-ends

**In-place modification (preserve relative order)** → same-direction

**Linked list** (middle, cycle, Kth from end) → same-direction

**Merge sorted sequences** → same-direction on each

**Three-way partition** → three pointers (Dutch flag)

**When NOT to use**

**Unsorted array without sorting first**
- Monotonicity argument breaks
- Use HashMap instead

**Random access patterns**
- Binary search or other techniques

**Problems where sortedness destroys needed info**
- Preserving original order matters

**Common pitfalls**

**1. Using two pointers on unsorted array**
- Won't find the answer
- Sort first or use HashMap

**2. Infinite loop when neither pointer moves**
- Ensure at least one pointer advances per iteration

**3. Off-by-one**
- Window size = right - left + 1 (inclusive)
- Loop condition left < right vs left <= right

**4. Duplicate handling in 3-sum**
- Must skip duplicates at each level for distinct triplets

**5. Wrong direction for container with most water**
- Must move the SHORTER side

**Relation to sliding window**
- Sliding window is a special case of same-direction two-pointer
- Both left and right advance, never decrease
- Windows are specifically contiguous ranges

**Recommendation:** Master both **opposite-ends** (convergent) and **same-direction** (tandem) variants — they handle different problem classes. For **opposite-ends**, always verify the array is **sorted** (or that monotonicity exists); otherwise the pointer-movement argument breaks. Practice the **canonical problems**: two-sum sorted, container with most water, 3-sum (outer loop + two-pointer), palindrome check, and Dutch national flag. For **same-direction**, the pattern is: **slow pointer marks the next write position, fast pointer scans** — this applies to remove duplicates, move zeros, and linked-list operations. For **linked lists**, know the **fast = 2×, slow = 1×** pattern for middle and cycle detection (see Floyd's algorithm). When tempted to use **two-pointer on an unsorted array**, ask: do I have monotonicity? If not, **sort first** (O(n log n)) or use a **HashMap** (O(n) space). The **3-sum** pattern — outer loop + two-pointer inner — generalizes to 4-sum and K-sum (recursion + two-pointer at base). Beware **duplicate handling**: explicit skips like `while (left < right && nums[left] == nums[left+1]) left++;` are essential for distinct-triplet problems. The **mental model**: **two-pointer = exploit sortedness/monotonicity to skip states**; **sliding window = same-direction two-pointer on contiguous ranges with stateful window**. Together these patterns handle a huge fraction of array/string interview problems in O(n) time.

questions.title: Fast and Slow Pointers — Floyd's Cycle Detection, Cycle Start, Middle
questions.direct_answer: **Fast and slow pointers** (a.k.a. **tortoise and hare**) use two pointers traversing a sequence at different speeds — typically one moving 1 step per iteration and the other moving 2 — to detect cycles, find middles, or measure positions in linked lists in **O(n) time and O(1) space**. **Cycle detection (Floyd's algorithm)**: start both pointers at head; advance `slow = slow.next` and `fast = fast.next.next`; if they **meet at the same node**, there's a cycle; if `fast` or `fast.next` becomes null, there's no cycle. **Why it works**: once both pointers are inside the cycle, the gap between them changes by 1 each iteration (fast gains 1 on slow); eventually the gap becomes a multiple of the cycle length, so they meet. **Finding cycle start**: after they meet, reset one pointer to head; advance both at the same speed (1 step); they meet exactly at the cycle start. **Why**: math shows the distance from meeting point to cycle start equals the distance from head to cycle start (both measured along pointers). **Finding middle**: move slow 1 step, fast 2 steps; when fast reaches end, slow is at the middle. **Other applications**: **happy number** (sum of squares of digits forms a cycle at 1 or not), **palindrome linked list** (find middle, reverse second half, compare), **find Kth from end** (two pointers, fast starts K ahead). **Why not use a HashSet?** Works (O(n) time, O(n) space) but two-pointer is more elegant and saves memory. **Edge cases**: empty list, single node, self-loop, very short lists. **Algorithmic note**: Floyd's is one of several cycle-detection algorithms; **Brent's algorithm** is slightly faster in practice (fewer pointer advancements) but harder to remember. For interviews, Floyd's is the expected answer.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows Floyd's algorithm, can prove why it works, can find the cycle start (second phase), and knows related applications (middle, Kth from end)
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Null-pointer exception when fast.next is null but you dereference fast.next.next. Not understanding why cycle-start detection works (the math). Confusing 'meeting point' with 'cycle start'
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Prove the algorithm's correctness with the distance math, mention Brent's algorithm, discuss happy number and palindrome LL applications, address the O(1) space advantage over HashSet

sections.title: Why Fast/Slow Pointers
sections.content:
Consider detecting a cycle in a linked list. The obvious approach uses a `HashSet<ListNode>`:
```java
Set<ListNode> seen = new HashSet<>();
while (head != null) {
    if (!seen.add(head)) return true;
    head = head.next;
}
return false;
```
This works in **O(n) time and O(n) space**.

**Floyd's algorithm (tortoise and hare)** achieves the same in **O(n) time and O(1) space**:
- `slow` moves one step at a time.
- `fast` moves two steps at a time.
- If there's a cycle, they will meet inside it.
- If there's no cycle, `fast` or `fast.next` will hit null.

**Why 1 and 2 speeds?** Once both are inside the cycle, the gap between them changes by exactly 1 per iteration (fast gains one step on slow). Eventually the gap is a multiple of the cycle length — meeting.

**The O(1) space** is the headline feature; it's what makes this elegant.

**General pattern — fast/slow pointers apply when**:
- You're traversing a sequence (linked list, string, array).
- You want to detect a cycle, find a midpoint, or measure positions relative to the end.
- You want O(1) space.

sections.title: Cycle Detection — Floyd's Algorithm
Finding the Cycle Start
Finding the Middle of a Linked List
Beyond Linked Lists — Happy Number
Floyd's vs Brent's vs HashSet
sections.content:
**Floyd's algorithm**
- Simple: 1-step vs 2-step.
- O(n) time, O(1) space.
- Well-known and easy to remember.
- Proof via distance math is elegant but takes a moment.

**Brent's algorithm**
- Teleport the slow pointer to fast's position at exponentially growing intervals.
- ~36% fewer pointer advances than Floyd's on average.
- Slightly better for very long cycles.
- Less well-known; often beyond interview scope.

**HashSet method**
- Track seen nodes in a HashSet.
- O(n) time, O(n) space.
- Simpler to explain and debug.
- Use when you don't care about space.

**When to use Floyd's in practice**
- Interviews (expected answer for cycle detection).
- Memory-constrained systems.
- Long sequences where O(n) space is prohibitive.

**When HashSet is fine**
- If you don't care about space.
- Problems where you need to remember which nodes were visited for other purposes.

**For cycle start**
- Floyd's two-phase algorithm is O(1) space, beautiful.
- HashSet: first node re-seen is the cycle start — trivially found.

**Performance note**: in practice, pointer chasing through a linked list is cache-unfriendly regardless of algorithm. The difference between Floyd's and Brent's is usually negligible; HashSet has allocation overhead that often makes Floyd's faster in raw wall-time for short lists too.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Fast/slow pointers**: two pointers at different speeds; classic 1/2 (tortoise/hare).
- **Floyd's cycle detection**: O(n) time, O(1) space; slow = 1 step, fast = 2 steps.
- **Cycle exists if** slow and fast meet.
- **No cycle if** fast reaches end (null).
- **Finding cycle start**: after meeting, reset one pointer to head; advance both at speed 1; they meet at cycle start.
- **Proof**: L (head to start) = kC - D (meeting point to start); follows from fast travels 2× slow's distance.
- **Finding middle**: standard fast=2×slow; even length returns second middle.
- **Kth from end**: fast starts K ahead; advance both until fast hits end.
- **Palindrome linked list**: find middle, reverse second half, compare (O(n) time, O(1) space).
- **Happy number**: apply Floyd's to sum-of-squares transition function.
- **Duplicate in [1..n] array of length n+1**: treat array as function, cycle start = duplicate.
- **Alternatives**: HashSet (O(n) space, simpler), Brent's algorithm (~36% fewer advances, less-known).
- **Edge cases**: empty list, single node, self-loop, very short lists.
- **Common bugs**: NPE on fast.next.next when fast.next is null; confusing meeting point with cycle start.
- **Space efficiency** is Floyd's main advantage over HashSet.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Fast/slow pointers** use two pointers at different speeds to detect cycles, find middles, or measure positions in linked lists — O(n) time, O(1) space.

**Floyd's cycle detection (tortoise and hare)**

- slow = head, fast = head
- Loop: slow = slow.next, fast = fast.next.next
- If fast or fast.next becomes null: no cycle
- If slow == fast: cycle detected

**Why it works**
- If no cycle: fast reaches end first
- If cycle: both eventually inside cycle; fast gains 1 on slow per iteration; gap becomes multiple of cycle length — they meet

**Finding cycle start (second phase)**

- After detection, reset one pointer to head
- Advance both at speed 1
- They meet at the cycle start

**The math (why it works)**
- L = distance head → cycle start
- C = cycle length
- D = distance cycle start → meeting point

- Slow traveled: L + D
- Fast traveled: L + D + kC (k extra laps)
- Fast = 2 × slow: 2(L + D) = L + D + kC
- So: L = kC - D
- Distance from head to start = distance from meeting point to start
- Walking both at speed 1 converges at start

**Finding the middle of a linked list**

- slow = head, fast = head
- slow = slow.next, fast = fast.next.next
- When fast reaches end: slow is at middle
- Even length: returns second middle (for first middle, start fast = head.next)

**Kth node from end**

- fast moves K steps first
- Then both move together until fast hits null
- slow is K from end
- O(n) single pass, O(1) space

**Palindrome linked list**

- Find middle with fast/slow
- Reverse second half
- Compare first half and reversed second half
- O(n) time, O(1) space
- Restore: re-reverse the second half if list must be preserved

**Happy number (cycle detection on integer sequence)**

- Sequence: n → sum of squares of digits
- If reaches 1: happy
- Else: cycle
- Apply Floyd's to the transformation function
- O(log n) per step, bounded iterations

**Find duplicate in [1..n] array of length n+1**

- Treat array as function f(i) = arr[i]
- Cycle must exist by pigeonhole
- Cycle start = the duplicate
- O(n) time, O(1) space (beats sorting or hashing)

**Alternatives**

**HashSet method**
- Track seen nodes/values in set
- O(n) time, O(n) space
- Simpler, but uses more memory
- First re-seen node = cycle start

**Brent's algorithm**
- Teleport slow pointer to fast at exponentially growing intervals
- ~36% fewer advances than Floyd's
- Less well-known
- Usually beyond interview scope

**Edge cases**

**Empty list**
- Return false / null

**Single node, no cycle**
- fast.next is null, loop exits, false

**Single node, self-loop**
- slow == fast after one step, true

**Two nodes, cycle**
- Correctly detected

**Common pitfalls**

**1. NPE on fast.next.next**
- Always check `fast != null && fast.next != null` before advancing

**2. Confusing meeting point with cycle start**
- They're different in general
- Need second phase to find cycle start

**3. Not understanding the math**
- Be ready to prove cycle start detection in interviews

**4. Off-by-one in middle**
- Even-length returns second middle by default
- Adjust initial fast pointer for first middle

**5. Using wrong initial pointers**
- Cycle start: start second pointer at head (not 'fast.next')

**Advantages of Floyd's over HashSet**

- O(1) space vs O(n)
- No allocation overhead
- Elegant, often interview-expected

**When HashSet is fine**
- You don't care about space
- You need to remember visited nodes for other purposes
- Code clarity matters more than memory efficiency

**Recommendation:** For **cycle detection on linked lists**, **Floyd's algorithm** is the expected interview answer — O(n) time, O(1) space. Memorize the **two-phase cycle start detection**: (1) slow/fast meet to detect the cycle; (2) reset one pointer to head, advance both at speed 1, they meet at the start. Be ready to **prove the math** (L = kC - D) because interviewers often ask why the second phase works. Know the **middle-finding variant** and its **palindrome linked list** application (find middle, reverse second half, compare) — both O(n) time, O(1) space. Know the **Kth from end** trick (fast starts K ahead, then both move together). Beyond linked lists, fast/slow detects cycles in any **deterministic state transition**: **happy number** (sum of squares of digits) and **find duplicate in [1..n] array** (treat array as function). The core insight: **any repeating process with a 'next' function can be cycle-detected with fast/slow in O(1) space**. For interviews, the **HashSet alternative** is acceptable but considered less elegant — use Floyd's when memory matters or for bonus points. Always handle **edge cases** (empty list, single node, self-loop) and check **`fast != null && fast.next != null`** before advancing to avoid NPE. The mental model: **two pointers, one twice as fast; if they ever meet, there's a cycle; if fast hits null, there isn't**. Simple, elegant, and applicable far beyond linked lists.

questions.question: Explain the top-K elements pattern using a heap in Java. How do you solve top-K frequent elements and K closest points? Why is complexity O(n log k)?
questions.title: Top-K Elements with a Heap — O(n log k) Pattern in Java
questions.direct_answer: **Top-K** problems ask for the K largest/smallest/most-frequent elements in a sequence. The **heap pattern** uses a **size-K heap** to track the top-K seen so far: iterate through all N elements, push into the heap; if the heap exceeds K, pop the 'worst' one. Final contents = the top K. **Complexity: O(n log k)** — each insertion/removal is O(log k), and we do it N times. **Space: O(k)**. **Key trick**: use the **opposite heap** — for top-K **largest**, use a **min-heap** (so the smallest is at the root and popped when exceeded); for top-K **smallest**, use a **max-heap**. This counter-intuitive pairing is the trick: we keep discarding the worst candidate in the heap. In Java: `PriorityQueue<>()` is min-heap by default; use `PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.reverseOrder())` for max-heap. **Why O(n log k) beats sorting (O(n log n))**: when k << n, log k << log n, so the heap approach is strictly better. For k ≈ n, both are similar. **Why it beats QuickSelect for streams/online**: QuickSelect is O(n) offline but requires the whole array; heap works for streaming data. **Common problems**: top-K frequent elements (use HashMap for counts, then heap over entries), K closest points to origin (heap keyed by distance), Kth largest element, top-K words. **Alternatives**: **QuickSelect** — O(n) average offline (partition-based, like quicksort), but worst-case O(n²) without careful pivot. **Sorting** — O(n log n), simplest. **Heap is best when**: data is streaming, online, or k is small relative to n. **Edge cases**: k > n (return all), ties (comparator decides, may need tiebreaker), empty input.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate can implement top-K with the correct heap type, explain the O(n log k) complexity, and compare with alternatives (QuickSelect, sorting)
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using max-heap for top-K largest (should be min-heap). Sorting first when heap is better. Not using HashMap for frequency-based problems
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Compare with QuickSelect O(n) and explain when streaming favors heap, mention custom Comparators for complex objects, discuss the pedagogical contradiction (min-heap for largest) clearly

sections.title: The Top-K Pattern
sections.content:
Given a stream or array of elements, find the K largest, smallest, or most-frequent ones.

**Naive approach — sort and take first K**: O(n log n).

**Heap approach — O(n log k)**:
- Maintain a size-K heap.
- For each element: push; if heap size > K, pop the worst.
- At the end, heap contains top K.

**The counter-intuitive trick — use the OPPOSITE heap type**:
- Top-K **largest** → **min-heap** (smallest at root; we pop it when new element is larger).
- Top-K **smallest** → **max-heap** (largest at root; pop when new element is smaller).
- Top-K **most frequent** → **min-heap** keyed by frequency.
- Top-K **most recent** → **min-heap** keyed by timestamp.

**Why**: the heap holds K 'winners so far'; the element to discard when a better one comes is the **worst winner** — so the heap root must be the worst. That's the opposite of what intuition suggests.

**Complexity**:
- **Time**: O(n log k) — each element × heap operation (log k).
- **Space**: O(k).

**When heap beats sorting**: when k << n. `log k` is much smaller than `log n`.

sections.title: Top-K Largest Numbers
Top-K Frequent Elements
K Closest Points to Origin
Top-K with Custom Comparator — Top K Words
Heap vs QuickSelect vs Sort
sections.content:
**Heap approach**
- **Time**: O(n log k).
- **Space**: O(k).
- **Pros**: works for streaming; simple; generic comparator.
- **Cons**: slower than QuickSelect offline for large k.

**QuickSelect (partition-based)**
- **Time**: O(n) average, O(n²) worst.
- **Space**: O(1) with in-place partitioning.
- **Pros**: fastest offline.
- **Cons**: in-place (destroys input); worst case; harder to explain; doesn't work for streaming.
- Use randomized pivot or introspective switch to HeapSelect to guarantee O(n).

**Full sort**
- **Time**: O(n log n).
- **Pros**: simplest code.
- **Cons**: slower than heap for small k; unnecessary work.

**Bucket sort** (for bounded integer frequencies)
- **Time**: O(n).
- **Space**: O(n).
- **Pros**: linear time.
- **Cons**: requires bounded range; doesn't work for arbitrary comparators.

**Decision**:
- **k << n, offline**: heap is fine (O(n log k)).
- **Large k ≈ n/2, offline, pure speed**: QuickSelect.
- **Streaming / online**: heap (only option).
- **Small n or simplicity matters**: just sort.
- **Bounded frequency range**: bucket sort for O(n).

**Java API notes**:
- `PriorityQueue<>()` is min-heap by default.
- `PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.reverseOrder())` for max-heap.
- `new PriorityQueue<>(k)` to hint initial capacity.
- `pq.offer(e)`, `pq.poll()`, `pq.peek()`.
- No indexed access; `contains` and `remove(obj)` are O(n).
- Not thread-safe — use `PriorityBlockingQueue` for concurrency.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Top-K pattern**: maintain size-K heap; push each element, pop when size > K.
- **Time O(n log k)**, **Space O(k)**.
- **Use OPPOSITE heap**: min-heap for top-K largest, max-heap for top-K smallest.
- **Heap root** must be the element to discard (the 'worst' by final ranking).
- **Top-K frequent**: HashMap for counts, then heap on entries.
- **K closest points**: max-heap on squared distance (no sqrt needed).
- **Top-K words with tiebreaker**: comparator must break ties in the reverse direction of final ranking.
- **Java PriorityQueue**: min-heap by default; use `Comparator.reverseOrder()` for max-heap.
- **Alternatives**: full sort (O(n log n)), QuickSelect (O(n) avg, O(n²) worst, in-place), bucket sort (O(n), bounded range).
- **Heap beats sorting when k << n**: log k << log n.
- **QuickSelect beats heap offline** for large k, but heap works for streaming.
- **Bucket sort** is linear but needs bounded frequency range.
- **PriorityQueue.contains is O(n)**: avoid for lookups; use HashMap alongside if needed.
- **Edge cases**: k > n, ties, empty input.
- **Streaming top-K**: heap is the only O(k) space option.
- **For single Kth value**: heap.peek() after iteration — the root is the Kth largest/smallest.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Top-K pattern** finds the K largest/smallest/most-frequent elements in O(n log k) time and O(k) space using a heap.

**The core idea**
- Maintain a size-K heap of winners so far
- For each element: push; if size exceeds K, pop the worst
- Final heap = top K

**Complexity**
- **Time: O(n log k)** — each push/pop is O(log k)
- **Space: O(k)**

**The counter-intuitive trick — opposite heap**

**Top-K LARGEST → MIN-heap**
- Smallest at root — that's what we pop when adding a larger element
- Heap root = worst of our current top-K

**Top-K SMALLEST → MAX-heap**
- Largest at root — pop when adding a smaller element

**Top-K MOST FREQUENT → min-heap keyed by frequency**

**Top-K MOST RECENT → min-heap keyed by timestamp**

Reasoning: heap root is what we discard when exceeding K — must be the 'worst by ranking'.

**Java PriorityQueue**
- **Default: min-heap**
- **Max-heap: `new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.reverseOrder())`**
- Ops: offer, poll, peek
- No random access; contains/remove are O(n)

**Examples**

**Kth largest element**
- Min-heap of size K
- peek() after iteration = Kth largest

**Top-K frequent elements**
- Step 1: HashMap of counts
- Step 2: min-heap of size K keyed by count
- Total: O(n + D log k) where D = distinct elements

**K closest points to origin**
- Max-heap of size K keyed by squared distance (no sqrt — ordering preserved)
- Top-K smallest distances → max-heap

**Top-K words with tie-break**
- Min-heap keyed by frequency
- Tiebreaker: larger lex at root (so it's popped)
- Result reversed at the end
- Tiebreaker direction is opposite of final desired ordering

**Alternative approaches**

**Sort (O(n log n))**
- Simplest
- Wasteful for small k
- Use for small n or simplicity

**QuickSelect (O(n) average, O(n²) worst)**
- Partition-based, like quicksort
- In-place, destroys input
- Fastest offline
- Randomize pivot to avoid worst case
- Doesn't work for streaming

**Bucket sort (O(n))**
- Only for bounded frequency range
- `buckets[freq] = list of elements`
- Linear time, O(n) space

**Heap**
- O(n log k) — best when k << n
- Works for **streaming / online** (only option)
- Generic comparator
- Simple to code

**Decision matrix**

**Small k, offline** → heap

**Large k ≈ n/2, pure speed** → QuickSelect

**Streaming / online** → heap

**Bounded frequency range** → bucket sort

**Simplicity** → sort

**Common pitfalls**

**1. Using max-heap for top-K largest**
- Wrong! Use min-heap
- Mental check: what needs to be popped when exceeding K? That's the heap root

**2. Sqrt on distances**
- Unnecessary; squared distance preserves ordering
- Avoids floating-point precision issues

**3. Wrong tiebreaker direction**
- Always think: 'what should be popped when two elements tie?'
- That's the worst by final ranking

**4. Using contains on PriorityQueue**
- O(n) — slow
- Use HashSet alongside if lookup needed

**5. Not hinting initial capacity**
- `new PriorityQueue<>(k)` avoids resize

**6. Missing edge cases**
- k > n: return all
- Empty input: return empty
- Ties: comparator must handle explicitly

**Streaming top-K**
- Heap is the only bounded-space option
- Maintain size-K heap as data flows in
- O(log k) per element amortized
- Used in real-time analytics, top-trends-now systems

**PriorityQueue vs TreeMap**
- PriorityQueue: fast for top-K, no random access
- TreeMap: sorted keys, ceiling/floor in O(log n), more flexible
- For top-K specifically, PriorityQueue is simpler

**Recommendation:** The **top-K heap pattern** is one of the most useful interview techniques — **O(n log k) time, O(k) space**. Memorize the **counter-intuitive rule**: use the **opposite heap type** — min-heap for top-K largest, max-heap for top-K smallest. The mental check: **the heap root is what gets popped when we exceed K, so it must be the worst by the final ranking**. For **frequency problems** (top-K frequent elements/words), combine **HashMap for counts** + **heap of size K**. For **distance problems** (K closest points), use **squared distance** (no sqrt) and a max-heap because we want the K smallest distances. For **tiebreaker problems** (top-K words with lex tiebreak), set the comparator so the element to discard is at the root — this often means the tiebreaker is in the **opposite direction** of the final ranking. Know the **alternatives**: **QuickSelect** is O(n) average offline but doesn't stream and has O(n²) worst case; **sorting** is O(n log n) — wasteful for small k; **bucket sort** is O(n) but needs bounded frequency range. Use **heap when k << n** or when data streams; use **QuickSelect for large-k offline speed**; use **sorting for simplicity**. In Java, `PriorityQueue<>()` is **min-heap by default** — use `Comparator.reverseOrder()` for max-heap. Avoid `contains`/`remove(obj)` (O(n)). The mental model: **top-K = size-K heap of winners, pop worst when overflow, time O(n log k)**. Once you recognize the pattern (find K best of something), the code writes itself.

The counter-intuitive trick — use the OPPOSITE heap type: Top-K largest → min-heap (smallest at root; we pop it when new element is larger). Top-K smallest → max-heap (largest at root; pop when new element is smaller). Top-K most frequent → min-heap keyed by frequency. Top-K most recent → min-heap keyed by timestamp. Why: the heap holds K 'winners so far'; the element to discard.

items: Using max-heap for top-K largest (should be min-heap)
Sorting first when heap is better
Not using HashMap for frequency-based problems

questions.question: Explain the backtracking pattern in Java. Solve subsets, permutations, combination sum, and N-queens. How do you prune the search space?
questions.title: Backtracking Pattern in Java — Subsets, Permutations, N-Queens, Pruning
questions.direct_answer: **Backtracking** is a brute-force search technique that **explores all possible solutions recursively**, **making choices** at each step and **undoing them (backtracking)** when a path fails or is complete. It's used for **combinatorial problems**: subsets, permutations, combinations, N-queens, Sudoku, word search, path-finding with constraints. **The template**: `solve(state) { if base case: record; for each choice: apply; solve; undo; }`. The 'undo' step is what distinguishes backtracking from plain recursion — we mutate a shared state (list, board, visited set) and restore it after the recursive call, saving memory. **Complexity** is typically exponential — O(2^n) for subsets, O(n!) for permutations, O(b^d) general (b = branching, d = depth) — but **pruning** (abandoning branches that can't yield a valid solution) is key to making it practical. **Canonical examples**: **Subsets** (2^n) — at each element, choose include or exclude; **Permutations** (n!) — track a `used[]` array; **Combination sum** — try each candidate, with pruning by remaining target; **N-queens** — try each column in each row, pruning via column/diagonal constraints. **Pruning techniques**: (1) **Invalid state detection** — return early if current partial state violates constraints (N-queens: conflicting queen); (2) **Bound-based pruning** — if best possible from here is worse than current best, abandon (branch-and-bound); (3) **Symmetry breaking** — avoid equivalent permutations (sort and skip duplicates); (4) **Ordering** — try promising candidates first to find a valid solution quickly. **When to use backtracking**: (1) need **all solutions** or **count** of solutions; (2) **constraint satisfaction**; (3) search space is **too large for DP** but structured enough to prune. **Don't use when**: greedy works (faster), DP applies (polynomial), or the problem is truly random. **Watch out**: shared-state mutation requires careful `add`/`remove` pairs; forgetting to undo is a classic bug.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate can apply the backtracking template, implement canonical examples (subsets, permutations, N-queens, combination sum), and recognize pruning opportunities
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting to undo the state mutation after recursion. Using separate lists per branch (wastes memory). Not pruning, leading to TLE. Forgetting duplicate-handling in combination/subset problems
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the template pattern generically, discuss several pruning techniques (invalid state, bound, symmetry, ordering), mention branch-and-bound for optimization variants, and contrast with DP

sections.title: The Backtracking Template
Subsets — 2^n Solutions
Permutations — n! Solutions
Combination Sum — with Pruning
N-Queens — Classic Constraint Satisfaction
Pruning Techniques
sections.content:
**1. Invalid state detection**
- Return early if the partial state violates constraints.
- N-queens: conflict check before placing.
- Sudoku: check row/column/box before placing.
- Word search: check out-of-bounds, visited cell.

**2. Bound-based pruning (branch-and-bound)**
- If the best possible outcome from here can't beat the current best, abandon.
- Classic in optimization (TSP, Knapsack exact solutions).
- Example: combination sum — `if (cand[i] > remaining) break;`.

**3. Symmetry breaking**
- Don't generate equivalent solutions.
- Subsets/permutations with duplicates: sort, skip duplicates at the same recursion level.
- N-queens: restrict first queen's column to avoid mirror-image solutions.

**4. Ordering (greedy hints)**
- Try promising choices first to find a valid solution quickly.
- Sudoku: try cells with fewest candidates first (most-constrained variable heuristic).
- A* search: prioritize low-cost branches.

**5. Memoization / DP hybrid**
- If subproblems overlap, cache them.
- Combination sum with target tracking — can sometimes memoize based on (start, remaining).
- Converts backtracking into top-down DP when overlap exists.

**6. Bitmask state**
- For small N, encode 'used' as a bitmask: `int used` instead of `boolean[]`.
- Faster copying; enables memoization on state.
- TSP: dp[current][visited_bitmask].

**When pruning fails**: backtracking becomes exponential. If the problem has no structure to prune (random constraints), it may be NP-hard in a fundamental sense and require approximation algorithms.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Backtracking template**: choose → recurse → undo. Shared mutable state saves memory.
- **For each recursion level**: iterate choices; apply; solve; undo.
- **Complexity**: exponential in general (2^n for subsets, n! for permutations).
- **Pruning is essential**: invalid state detection, bound-based, symmetry breaking, ordering.
- **Canonical problems**: subsets, permutations, combinations, combination sum, N-queens, Sudoku, word search, restore IP addresses, generate parentheses.
- **Subsets**: use `start` index to avoid reusing; result includes every recursion-tree node.
- **Permutations**: use `used[]` or in-place swap; recursion ends at `size == n`.
- **Duplicates**: sort first, skip duplicates at same level (`if (i > start && nums[i] == nums[i-1]) continue`).
- **Combination sum (unlimited reuse)**: recurse with `i` (not `i+1`).
- **N-queens**: track `int[] queens` where queens[row] = col; validate column and diagonals.
- **Faster N-queens**: bitmasks or 3 boolean arrays for O(1) validity check.
- **Copy on record**: always `new ArrayList<>(current)` when adding to result (mutable shared state).
- **Undo the mutation**: `current.remove(current.size() - 1)` after recursion.
- **Early termination**: return on first success if only one solution needed.
- **Branch and bound**: backtracking + bound pruning for optimization problems.
- **Memoization hybrid**: if subproblems overlap, cache; may convert to DP.
- **Contrast with DP**: DP for polynomial; backtracking for exponential with pruning.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Backtracking** is a brute-force search that explores all possible solutions recursively, making choices and undoing them when a path fails or completes.

**The template**
1. **If base case** (solution complete): record and return
2. **For each choice**:
   - Check validity (prune if invalid)
   - Apply choice (mutate state)
   - Recurse
   - Undo choice (restore state)

**Why 'undo'?**
- Avoids copying full state at each call
- Shared mutable state is memory-efficient
- 'Undo' is what distinguishes backtracking from plain recursion

**Typical state**
- Current path (ArrayList)
- Used flags (boolean[])
- Board state (2D array)
- Visited set

**Complexity**
- 2^n for subsets
- n! for permutations
- b^d general (branching × depth)
- **Pruning is essential** to make practical

**Canonical problems**

**Subsets (2^n)**
- Each element: include or exclude
- Use `start` index to avoid reusing
- Every recursion-tree node is a valid subset (record at entry)

**Permutations (n!)**
- Try each unused element at each position
- Track with used[] array
- Base case: current.size() == n

**Combination sum**
- Unlimited reuse: recurse with `i` (not `i+1`)
- Sort + early break on target exceeded (pruning)

**N-queens**
- Place one queen per row, try each column
- Prune: validate column + both diagonals
- Faster: three boolean arrays (cols, diag1, diag2)

**Pruning techniques**

**1. Invalid state detection**
- Check constraints before recursing
- N-queens conflict check

**2. Bound-based (branch and bound)**
- Upper bound on best achievable
- Abandon if can't beat current best
- TSP, exact knapsack

**3. Symmetry breaking**
- Skip duplicates (subsets/permutations with repeats)
- N-queens: restrict first queen to half board

**4. Ordering**
- Try promising choices first
- Most-constrained variable heuristic (Sudoku)
- A* search

**5. Memoization**
- If subproblems overlap: cache
- Sometimes converts backtracking to DP

**6. Bitmask state**
- Small N: encode 'used' as int bitmask
- Fast copy; enables memoization
- TSP with dp[current][visited]

**Duplicate handling**
- Sort first
- Skip: `if (i > start && nums[i] == nums[i-1]) continue;`
- For permutations: `if (i > 0 && nums[i] == nums[i-1] && !used[i-1]) continue;`
- Ensures canonical order, eliminates duplicates

**Common pitfalls**

**1. Forgetting to undo**
- `current.remove(current.size() - 1)` after recursion
- Without this: accumulating state across branches — wrong answers

**2. Copying separate state per branch**
- Wastes memory
- Use shared mutable state with undo

**3. Forgetting to copy on record**
- `result.add(current)` vs `result.add(new ArrayList<>(current))`
- First adds reference; later mutations corrupt the recorded answer
- Always copy

**4. No pruning**
- Time limit exceeded
- Add early returns, bound checks, sort + skip

**5. Wrong index passing**
- Subsets: `i + 1` (no reuse)
- Combination sum (unlimited): `i`
- Permutations: no start index, just used[]

**6. Off-by-one in base case**
- Subsets: record at every entry (all sizes)
- Permutations: record when size == n
- Combinations: record when we hit target size or sum

**When to use backtracking**

**Good fit**
- All solutions or count
- Constraint satisfaction (Sudoku, N-queens)
- Small n, structured pruning
- Tree/graph search with backtrack (word search)

**Not a good fit**
- Polynomial solution exists (DP, greedy)
- Problem is truly random (no pruning possible)
- Pure optimization with linear structure (greedy)

**Backtracking vs DP**
- DP: polynomial, overlapping subproblems, optimization
- Backtracking: exponential, combinatorial, all-solutions
- Hybrid: backtracking with memoization (when subproblems overlap)

**Backtracking vs BFS/DFS**
- DFS without undo: visits once, can't revisit
- Backtracking: revisits after undo (different paths)
- BFS: finds shortest path, different problem class

**Branch and bound**
- Backtracking + upper/lower bound pruning
- For optimization: TSP, exact 0/1 knapsack
- Uses fractional knapsack as bound

**Recommendation:** Master the **backtracking template** — choose, recurse, undo — because it applies to a huge class of combinatorial problems: subsets, permutations, combinations, N-queens, Sudoku, word search, generate parentheses, restore IP addresses. The **essence is the 'undo'** step; without it, you're doing plain recursion and wasting memory via state copies. Always **copy when recording** (`new ArrayList<>(current)`) because the current state mutates. For **problems with duplicate elements**, sort first and skip duplicates at each level — either `if (i > start && nums[i] == nums[i-1])` for subsets/combinations or `if (i > 0 && nums[i] == nums[i-1] && !used[i-1])` for permutations. For **unlimited reuse** (combination sum), recurse with `i`, not `i+1`. **Pruning** is what makes backtracking practical — use **invalid state detection** (abandon violating branches), **bound-based pruning** (branch-and-bound for optimization), **symmetry breaking** (canonical ordering), and **smart ordering** (most-constrained-variable first). For **N-queens**, track `queens[row] = col` and validate columns and both diagonals; use three boolean arrays for O(1) validity. When **subproblems overlap**, add memoization — backtracking morphs into top-down DP. Don't reach for backtracking when **greedy or DP** would work faster; backtracking is for when the search space is fundamentally combinatorial and pruning can prevent exponential blow-up. The mental model: **backtracking = DFS of the decision tree with state mutation and undo**. Master the template, then recognize it everywhere combinatorial search is needed.
